Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.

- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)

1	Build `csvledger`, a small Python command-line tool that reads one or more bank-export CSV files of transactions, assigns each transaction a category using a rules file, and prints a monthly report. It must run as `python -m csvledger` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Provide two commands: `report` (per-month, per-category totals) and `categorize` (each transaction with its assigned category). Both commands print either an aligned text table or JSON. Money must be exact (no floating point) and output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. Identical transactions repeated across overlapping exports must be counted once. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
2

1	# csvledger: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `csvledger/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
7	- **Entry point:** `python -m csvledger <command> ...` run from repo root.
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1** `python -m csvledger` exposes subcommands `report` and `categorize`; `--help` exits 0.
12	- **R2** Transaction files are parsed per the CSV contract; any invalid file or row aborts the run with exit 3 and no stdout.
13	- **R3** The rules file is parsed per the rules contract; any invalid rule aborts with exit 4 and no stdout.
14	- **R4** Each transaction gets exactly one category: the highest-priority matching rule; ties go to the rule earliest in the file; no match gives `Uncategorized`.
15	- **R5** Duplicate transactions (same date, stripped description, and numeric amount value) across all inputs are kept once (first occurrence) and a warning is written to stderr. Deduplication runs over all rows of all input files before the `--month` filter; the warning count N covers duplicates across all inputs regardless of `--month`.
16	- **R6** `report` aggregates by month and category: count, income, expenses, net.
17	- **R7** `categorize` lists every transaction, sorted by date ascending, ties in input order.
18	- **R8** `--month YYYY-MM` restricts both commands to transactions in that month.
19	- **R9** `--format table|json` selects output; default `table`.
20	- **R10** Money uses `decimal.Decimal`; sums are exact; displayed values are rounded once to 2 dp, ROUND_HALF_UP, never shown as `-0.00`.
21	- **R11** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, stable ordering, no locale use.
22	
23	## Interface contract
24	
25	### Commands
26	
27	```
28	python -m csvledger report     [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
29	python -m csvledger categorize [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
30	```
31	
32	- `FILE`: one or more transaction CSV paths, processed in argument order. `-` is an ordinary file name; stdin is never read.
33	- `--rules`: optional. When omitted, every transaction is `Uncategorized`.
34	- `--month`: must match `^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$`, else usage error.
35	- argparse `prog` is `csvledger`. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
36	- Load order: rules file first, then transaction files in argument order. First error wins.
37	
38	### Exit codes
39	
40	| Code | Meaning |
41	|---|---|
42	| 0 | Success (including empty result and duplicate warnings) |
43	| 1 | Reserved for unexpected internal error; never intentional |
44	| 2 | Usage error (argparse: unknown flag, missing FILE, bad `--format`/`--month`) |
45	| 3 | Transaction file error |
46	| 4 | Rules file error |
47	
48	### Transaction CSV
49	
50	- Encoding UTF-8, optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`); opened with `newline=""`; parsed with `csv.reader` defaults (comma, `"` quoting).
51	- Line 1 is the header. Header names are stripped and lowercased; `date`, `description`, `amount` are required, in any order; extra columns are ignored; duplicate names are an error.
52	- Rows with zero fields (blank lines) are skipped. Every other row must have exactly as many fields as the header.
53	- `date`: stripped value must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a valid calendar date (regex first; do not rely on `date.fromisoformat` alone).
54	- `amount`: stripped value must match `^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$`. Negative = expense (outflow), positive = income, zero counts but adds to neither.
55	- `description`: stripped; may be empty.
56	- A header-only file is valid (zero transactions). A file with no header line (0 bytes) is an error.
57	
58	### Rules CSV
59	
60	- Same encoding/header/blank-row/field-count rules. Required columns: `category`, `type`, `pattern`, `priority`.
61	- `category`: stripped, non-empty. `type`: stripped, exactly `contains` or `regex`. `pattern`: stripped, non-empty. `priority`: stripped, matches `^-?\d+$`.
62	- `contains`: `pattern.casefold() in description.casefold()`.
63	- `regex`: `re.search(pattern, description, re.IGNORECASE)`; compiled at load time.
64	- Zero rules is valid.
65	
66	### Money formatting
67	
68	`q = value.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_HALF_UP)`; if `q == 0` print `0.00`; otherwise `format(q, "f")`. Aggregates (income, expenses, net, month totals) are summed unrounded, then formatted. `net = income_raw + expenses_raw`.
69	
70	### `report` table
71	
72	Columns, in order: `MONTH` (left), `CATEGORY` (left), `COUNT` (right), `INCOME` (right), `EXPENSES` (right), `NET` (right). Width of each column = max(len(header), longest value) using `len()` on code points. Cells joined by two spaces; each line right-stripped. Line 1: headers. Line 2: dashes of each column width. Then one row per (month, category), sorted by month ascending then category by code-point ascending. No total rows. Zero transactions: header and dash line only.
73	
74	### `categorize` table
75	
76	Columns: `DATE` (left), `AMOUNT` (right, per-transaction amount formatted as money), `CATEGORY` (left), `DESCRIPTION` (left). Same width, separator, dash-line and right-strip rules.
77	
78	### JSON
79	
80	`json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` followed by `\n`. Money values are strings; counts are integers. Key order is exactly as shown.
81	
82	- `report`: `{"months": [{"month", "count", "income", "expenses", "net", "categories": [{"category", "count", "income", "expenses", "net"}]}]}`. Months and categories sorted as in the table.
83	- `categorize`: `{"transactions": [{"date", "description", "amount", "category"}]}`.
84	- Empty: `{"months": []}` / `{"transactions": []}`.
85	
86	## Error handling
87	
88	Errors go to stderr as one line, prefix `csvledger: error: `, then exit with the code shown; stdout stays empty. `<path>` is exactly the argv string given on the command line (a relative path stays relative); `<line>` is `csv.reader.line_num` after reading the record. Row checks run in this order: field count, date, amount (transactions) or field count, category, type, pattern, priority, regex (rules). Header checks run in this order: (1) no header line, (2) duplicate column, (3) missing required column. For a duplicate column, `<name>` is the second occurrence after strip and lowercase, and the first duplicate in header order is reported. For a missing column, `<name>` is the first absent name in the listed order.
89	
90	| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
91	|---|---|---|
92	| File missing/unreadable | 3 / 4 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
93	| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 / 4 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
94	| No header line | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing header` |
95	| Duplicate header name (first duplicate in header order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: duplicate column '<name>'` |
96	| Required column absent (first in listed order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing column '<name>'` |
97	| Field count mismatch | 3 / 4 | `<path>:<line>: expected <N> fields, got <M>` |
98	| Bad date | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid date '<value>'` |
99	| Bad amount | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid amount '<value>'` |
100	| Empty category / pattern | 4 | `<path>:<line>: empty category` / `empty pattern` |
101	| Bad type | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid type '<value>'` |
102	| Bad priority | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid priority '<value>'` |
103	| Regex fails to compile | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid regex '<pattern>'` |
104	| argparse usage errors | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match the regex `^csvledger( report\| categorize)?: error: ` (argparse subparser prog form allowed) |
105	
106	Warning (exit unaffected): `csvledger: warning: skipped <N> duplicate row(s)` when N > 0, written after stdout output. `<value>` is the stripped field value.
107	
108	## Acceptance criteria
109

## `TextIOWrapper.reconfigure`

**Signature:**

```python
reconfigure(*, encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None,
            line_buffering=None, write_through=None)
```

All parameters are keyword-only (the `*`). Added in 3.7. Since 3.11, `encoding="locale"` is supported.

**Constraints:**

- **Unspecified parameters keep their current settings**, with one exception: `errors='strict'` is used when `encoding` is given but `errors` is not.
- **`encoding` and `newline` cannot be changed after data has been read** from the stream. Changing `encoding` after a write is allowed.
- **An implicit stream flush** happens before the new parameters are set.

## Newline write translation

The `newline` argument accepts `None`, `''`, `'\n'`, `'\r'`, or `'\r\n'`. When writing:

- **`None`**: any `'\n'` written is translated to the system default line separator, `os.linesep`.
- **`''` or `'\n'`**: no translation takes place.
- **Any other legal value** (`'\r'` or `'\r\n'`): each `'\n'` written is translated to that string.

Example (illustrative, not from the page):

```python
import io, os

buf = io.BytesIO()
f = io.TextIOWrapper(buf, encoding="utf-8", newline=None)
f.write("a\nb")          # '\n' becomes os.linesep on write
f.flush()
# buf.getvalue() == ("a" + os.linesep + "b").encode("utf-8")

f.reconfigure(newline="\r\n")   # subsequent '\n' writes become '\r\n'
```

The visible portion of the page covers `sys.stdin`, `sys.stdout`, and `sys.stderr` in the section that starts "[File objects] used by the interpreter..." Some of what you asked for isn't in that text.

**Encoding and error handling**

- The encoding and error handler are initialized from `PyConfig.stdio_encoding` and `PyConfig.stdio_errors`.
- On Windows, UTF-8 is used for the console device. Disk files and pipes use the system locale encoding (the ANSI codepage). Non-console character devices such as `NUL` use the console input and output codepages at startup, for stdin and stdout/stderr respectively. This defaults to the system locale encoding if the process wasn't initially attached to a console.
- Setting the environment variable `PYTHONLEGACYWINDOWSSTDIO` changes the Windows console behavior so the console codepages are used as for any other character device.
- On all platforms, you can override the encoding with the `PYTHONIOENCODING` environment variable, or with `-X utf8` / `PYTHONUTF8`. On Windows console, this override only applies when `PYTHONLEGACYWINDOWSSTDIO` is also set.

**stderr error handler**

The page does not say that `stderr` defaults to `backslashreplace`. The only `backslashreplace` mention in this excerpt is in the `sys.displayhook` section. There, if `repr(value)` can't be encoded to `sys.stdout.encoding` with `sys.stdout.errors`, it is encoded with `'backslashreplace'` instead. The `displayhook` change note says this was added in 3.2. The stream's actual default error handler comes from `PyConfig.stdio_errors`, which this page doesn't document.

**Buffering and newlines**

- `stdout` is line-buffered when interactive and block-buffered otherwise.
- `stderr` is line-buffered in both cases. Since 3.9, non-interactive `stderr` is line-buffered instead of fully buffered.
- `-u` or `PYTHONUNBUFFERED` makes both streams unbuffered.
- The page says nothing about newline translation for `sys.stdout`.

**reconfigure**

**Other notes**

- For binary I/O, use the underlying buffer, e.g. `sys.stdout.buffer.write(b'abc')`.
- Library code should not assume the standard streams support `.buffer`, because they may be replaced with objects such as `io.StringIO`.
- `sys.__stdin__`, `sys.__stdout__`, and `sys.__stderr__` can be `None`, for example in Windows GUI apps without a console or in apps started with `pythonw`.

## `json.dumps()` formatting options

**`indent`** (int, str, or None; default `None`)
- A positive integer indents that many spaces per level. A string such as `"\t"` is used for each level.
- Zero, negative, or `""` inserts only newlines.
- `None` (the default) produces the most compact output with no newlines.

**`separators`** (default depends on `indent`)
- Default is `(', ', ': ')` when `indent` is `None`, and `(',', ': ')` otherwise. The change to `(',', ': ')` for indented output was made in 3.4.
- For the most compact output, use `(',', ':')`.

**`ensure_ascii`** (default `True`)
- `True` escapes all non-ASCII and non-printable characters.
- `False` outputs characters as-is, except the quotation mark, reverse solidus, and control characters U+0000 through U+001F, which are always escaped.

**`sort_keys`** (default `False`)
- `True` outputs dictionaries sorted by key.
- Keys are sorted before being converted to strings, so numeric keys sort by value, not by their string form.

**Key ordering**
- By default, encoders preserve input order. Order is lost only if the underlying containers are unordered.

## Examples from the page

```python
>>> print(json.dumps({'6': 7, '4': 5}, sort_keys=True, indent=4))
{
    "4": 5,
    "6": 7
}

>>> json.dumps([1, 2, 3, {'4': 5, '6': 7}], separators=(',', ':'))
'[1,2,3,{"4":5,"6":7}]'

>>> json.dumps(1 + 2j, default=custom_json)
'{"__complex__": true, "real": 1.0, "imag": 2.0}'

>>> json.dumps("\u1234")   # ensure_ascii=True by default
'"\\u1234"'
```

## NaN and infinity

- By default (`allow_nan=True`), `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity` are output. This is not valid JSON.
- With `allow_nan=False`, serializing these floats raises `ValueError`.

```python
>>> json.dumps(float('-inf'))
'-Infinity'
>>> json.dumps(float('nan'))
'NaN'
```

## Not covered on this page

- **Float repr:** The page shows floats like `1.0` and `2.0` in output but does not document the formatting rule. In CPython, floats are generally written using `float.__repr__`, which gives the shortest string that round-trips. Check the CPython source or `float.__repr__` documentation to confirm.
- **Trailing newline:** `dumps()` returns a string with no trailing newline. The page's `print()` examples add one, and the command-line tool's output ends with a newline. This is inferred from the examples, not stated.
- **Empty list and dict with `indent`:** The page does not cover this. In CPython, `json.dumps([], indent=4)` returns `'[]'` and `json.dumps({}, indent=4)` returns `'{}'`, with no inner newlines. This is based on known behavior, not on this page.

### error() behavior and exit status
- The visible text doesn't document `error()` directly. The `exit_on_error` section says that on invalid arguments, `parse_args()` "will print a *message* to `sys.stderr` and exit with a status code of 2."
- Error output follows a usage line followed by `PROG: error: <msg>`:

```
>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='PROG')
>>> parser.add_argument('--foo', type=int)
>>> parser.parse_args(['--foo', 'spam'])
usage: PROG [-h] [--foo FOO]
PROG: error: argument --foo: invalid int value: 'spam'
```

### `prog`
- Default: derived from how `__main__` was run. It is the base name of `sys.argv[0]` for a file, the interpreter name plus `sys.argv[0]` for a directory or zipfile, or the interpreter name plus `-m` plus the module name for `-m`.
- Override with `prog=`. Use `%(prog)s` in help text to reference it.
- Changed in 3.14: the default now reflects how `__main__` was actually executed.

```
>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='myprogram')
>>> parser.add_argument('--foo', help='foo of the %(prog)s program')
```

### `exit_on_error`
- Default `True`. Setting it to `False` lets you catch errors yourself:

```
>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(exit_on_error=False)
>>> parser.add_argument('--integers', type=int)
>>> try:
...     parser.parse_args('--integers a'.split())
... except argparse.ArgumentError:
...     print('Catching an argumentError')
...
Catching an argumentError
```

- Added in 3.9.

### `-` handling
- The visible text does not describe `-` as a plain positional argument. Its documented behavior is with `FileType`: `'-'` maps to `sys.stdin` for readable files and `sys.stdout` for writable ones.

```
>>> parser.add_argument('infile', type=argparse.FileType('r'))
>>> parser.parse_args(['-'])
Namespace(infile=<_io.TextIOWrapper name='<stdin>' encoding='UTF-8'>)
```

- `'--'` ends option parsing, so later arguments are positional: `parser.parse_args(['--', '-f'])` gives `foo='-f'`.

### `type=` callables
- The callable takes a single string. If it raises `ArgumentTypeError`, `TypeError`, or `ValueError`, argparse catches it and shows a formatted error. Other exception types are not handled.

```
>>> def hyphenated(string):
...     return '-'.join([word[:4] for word in string.casefold().split()])
...
>>> parser.add_argument('short_title', type=hyphenated)
```

- `type` is applied to `default` only when the default is a string.
- `choices` are checked after type conversion.
- The page recommends keeping `type` for simple conversions and doing complex validation after parsing.

### Subparsers: `required` and `dest`
- `add_subparsers(required=...)` is keyword-only, defaults to `False`, and was added in 3.7.
- `dest` defaults to `None`, meaning no value is stored. Setting it records the chosen subcommand name:

```
>>> subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest='subparser_name')
>>> subparser1 = subparsers.add_parser('1')
>>> subparser2 = subparsers.add_parser('2')
>>> parser.parse_args(['2', 'frobble'])
Namespace(subparser_name='2', y='frobble')
```

- Used with `required=True`, the subparser is mandatory. The visible text doesn't show the error message for a missing subcommand.
- Subparser `set_defaults(func=...)` is the common pattern for dispatching.

### Help exit status
- The `'help'` action prints the full help for the current parser and exits. The visible text doesn't state the exit code (it is normally 0, but I can't confirm that from this page).

### `add_subparsers` `prog`
- Default: the program name plus any positional arguments that appear before the subparser argument.
- Changed in 3.14: a subparser's `prog` is no longer affected by a custom `usage=` in the main parser.
- The docs recommend passing `prog` to `add_subparsers()`, or `prog` and `usage` to `add_parser()`, when the main parser has a custom usage, to keep prefixes consistent.

### `metavar`
- Positional arguments display their `dest`. Optional arguments display the uppercased `dest`.
- `metavar` changes only the display name, not the attribute name.
- A tuple sets a separate display name for each value, for example `metavar=('bar', 'baz')` with `nargs=2`.
- Subcommands with no `metavar` display as `{cmd1,cmd2,...}`.
- Formatted `choices` override the default metavar.

## `subprocess.run()` Key Arguments

```python
subprocess.run(args, *, stdin=None, input=None, stdout=None, stderr=None,
               capture_output=False, shell=False, cwd=None, timeout=None,
               check=False, encoding=None, errors=None, text=None,
               env=None, universal_newlines=None, **other_popen_kwargs)
```

Per the docs, `run()` waits for the command to finish and returns a `CompletedProcess` instance. `timeout`, `input`, `check`, and `capture_output` are handled by `run()` itself and are not passed to `Popen`.

### `args`
- Required. Should be a sequence of program arguments, which is generally preferred because the module handles quoting and escaping.
- A string is allowed only with `shell=True`, or when it names a program with no arguments.

### `capture_output`
- If true, stdout and stderr are captured, with both set to `PIPE` internally.
- Cannot be combined with `stdout` or `stderr`.
- To merge both streams, use `stdout=PIPE, stderr=STDOUT` instead.

```python
r = subprocess.run(["ls", "-l", "/dev/null"], capture_output=True)
print(r.stdout)  # b'crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 1, 3 ... /dev/null\n'
print(r.stderr)  # b''
```

### `text` / `encoding` / `errors` (and `universal_newlines`)
- Setting `encoding`, `errors`, or `text=True` opens stdin, stdout, and stderr in text mode. Without these, streams are binary.
- `text` was added in 3.7 as a clearer alias for `universal_newlines`, which is kept for backward compatibility.
- If `encoding` or `errors` is not given, the `io.TextIOWrapper` defaults apply.
- Line endings:
  - **stdout/stderr:** all line endings in the output are converted to `'\n'`. This is the universal-newlines behavior that normalizes `\r\n` (and `\r`) to `\n`.
  - **stdin:** `'\n'` in `input` is converted to `os.linesep`.
- In text mode, `input` must be `str`, and `stdout`/`stderr` in `CompletedProcess` are `str`.

```python
r = subprocess.run(["printf", "a\\r\\nb\\r\\n"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(repr(r.stdout))  # 'a\nb\n'
```

### Bytes mode (default)
- With none of `text`, `encoding`, `errors`, or `universal_newlines` set, `stdout`/`stderr` are `bytes`.
- No encoding or line-ending conversion is performed, so `\r\n` stays as-is.
- `input` must be a bytes sequence.
- Decoding is left to the application, since the encoding depends on the command.

```python
r = subprocess.run(["ls", "-l", "/dev/null"], capture_output=True)
data = r.stdout.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
```

### `cwd`
- Changes the child's working directory before execution. Accepts a string, bytes, or path-like object (bytes on Windows since 3.8).
- On POSIX, a relative executable path is resolved relative to `cwd`.

### `env`
- If not `None`, this mapping replaces the inherited environment entirely.
- Use `str` to `str` on any platform, or `bytes` to `bytes` on POSIX.
- It must include every variable the program needs.
- On Windows, side-by-side assemblies require a valid `%SystemRoot%` in `env`.

```python
import os
env = {**os.environ, "MY_VAR": "1"}  # copy, then add a variable
subprocess.run(["env"], env=env, text=True)
```

### `check`
- If true and the exit code is non-zero, raises `CalledProcessError`, which has `returncode`, `cmd`, `output`/`stdout`, and `stderr`.

```python
try:
    subprocess.run(["false"], check=True)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print(e.returncode)
```

### `timeout`
- Seconds, passed to `Popen.communicate()`.
- On expiry, the child is killed and waited for, then `TimeoutExpired` is raised. Its `output`/`stdout` and `stderr` attributes hold any captured output, as bytes regardless of `text`, or `None` if nothing was observed.
- Process creation itself may not be interruptible, so a timeout exception may come later than expected.

```python
try:
    subprocess.run(["sleep", "10"], timeout=2)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as e:
    print("timed out after", e.timeout, "s")
```

1	Build `csvledger`, a small Python command-line tool that reads one or more bank-export CSV files of transactions, assigns each transaction a category using a rules file, and prints a monthly report. It must run as `python -m csvledger` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Provide two commands: `report` (per-month, per-category totals) and `categorize` (each transaction with its assigned category). Both commands print either an aligned text table or JSON. Money must be exact (no floating point) and output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. Identical transactions repeated across overlapping exports must be counted once. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
2

1	# csvledger: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `csvledger/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
7	- **Entry point:** `python -m csvledger <command> ...` run from repo root.
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1** `python -m csvledger` exposes subcommands `report` and `categorize`; `--help` exits 0.
12	- **R2** Transaction files are parsed per the CSV contract; any invalid file or row aborts the run with exit 3 and no stdout.
13	- **R3** The rules file is parsed per the rules contract; any invalid rule aborts with exit 4 and no stdout.
14	- **R4** Each transaction gets exactly one category: the highest-priority matching rule; ties go to the rule earliest in the file; no match gives `Uncategorized`.
15	- **R5** Duplicate transactions (same date, stripped description, and numeric amount value) across all inputs are kept once (first occurrence) and a warning is written to stderr. Deduplication runs over all rows of all input files before the `--month` filter; the warning count N covers duplicates across all inputs regardless of `--month`.
16	- **R6** `report` aggregates by month and category: count, income, expenses, net.
17	- **R7** `categorize` lists every transaction, sorted by date ascending, ties in input order.
18	- **R8** `--month YYYY-MM` restricts both commands to transactions in that month.
19	- **R9** `--format table|json` selects output; default `table`.
20	- **R10** Money uses `decimal.Decimal`; sums are exact; displayed values are rounded once to 2 dp, ROUND_HALF_UP, never shown as `-0.00`.
21	- **R11** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, stable ordering, no locale use.
22	
23	## Interface contract
24	
25	### Commands
26	
27	```
28	python -m csvledger report     [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
29	python -m csvledger categorize [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
30	```
31	
32	- `FILE`: one or more transaction CSV paths, processed in argument order. `-` is an ordinary file name; stdin is never read.
33	- `--rules`: optional. When omitted, every transaction is `Uncategorized`.
34	- `--month`: must match `^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$`, else usage error.
35	- argparse `prog` is `csvledger`. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
36	- Load order: rules file first, then transaction files in argument order. First error wins.
37	
38	### Exit codes
39

## `TextIOWrapper.reconfigure`

**Signature:**

```python
reconfigure(*, encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None,
            line_buffering=None, write_through=None)
```

All parameters are keyword-only (the `*`). Added in 3.7. Since 3.11, `encoding="locale"` is supported.

**Constraints:**

- **Unspecified parameters keep their current settings**, with one exception: `errors='strict'` is used when `encoding` is given but `errors` is not.
- **`encoding` and `newline` cannot be changed after data has been read** from the stream. Changing `encoding` after a write is allowed.
- **An implicit stream flush** happens before the new parameters are set.

## Newline write translation

The `newline` argument accepts `None`, `''`, `'\n'`, `'\r'`, or `'\r\n'`. When writing:

- **`None`**: any `'\n'` written is translated to the system default line separator, `os.linesep`.
- **`''` or `'\n'`**: no translation takes place.
- **Any other legal value** (`'\r'` or `'\r\n'`): each `'\n'` written is translated to that string.

Example (illustrative, not from the page):

```python
import io, os

buf = io.BytesIO()
f = io.TextIOWrapper(buf, encoding="utf-8", newline=None)
f.write("a\nb")          # '\n' becomes os.linesep on write
f.flush()
# buf.getvalue() == ("a" + os.linesep + "b").encode("utf-8")

f.reconfigure(newline="\r\n")   # subsequent '\n' writes become '\r\n'
```

## `json.dumps()` formatting options

**`indent`** (int, str, or None; default `None`)
- A positive integer indents that many spaces per level. A string such as `"\t"` is used for each level.
- Zero, negative, or `""` inserts only newlines.
- `None` (the default) produces the most compact output with no newlines.

**`separators`** (default depends on `indent`)
- Default is `(', ', ': ')` when `indent` is `None`, and `(',', ': ')` otherwise. The change to `(',', ': ')` for indented output was made in 3.4.
- For the most compact output, use `(',', ':')`.

**`ensure_ascii`** (default `True`)
- `True` escapes all non-ASCII and non-printable characters.
- `False` outputs characters as-is, except the quotation mark, reverse solidus, and control characters U+0000 through U+001F, which are always escaped.

**`sort_keys`** (default `False`)
- `True` outputs dictionaries sorted by key.
- Keys are sorted before being converted to strings, so numeric keys sort by value, not by their string form.

**Key ordering**
- By default, encoders preserve input order. Order is lost only if the underlying containers are unordered.

## Examples from the page

```python
>>> print(json.dumps({'6': 7, '4': 5}, sort_keys=True, indent=4))
{
    "4": 5,
    "6": 7
}

>>> json.dumps([1, 2, 3, {'4': 5, '6': 7}], separators=(',', ':'))
'[1,2,3,{"4":5,"6":7}]'

>>> json.dumps(1 + 2j, default=custom_json)
'{"__complex__": true, "real": 1.0, "imag": 2.0}'

>>> json.dumps("\u1234")   # ensure_ascii=True by default
'"\\u1234"'
```

## NaN and infinity

- By default (`allow_nan=True`), `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity` are output. This is not valid JSON.
- With `allow_nan=False`, serializing these floats raises `ValueError`.

```python
>>> json.dumps(float('-inf'))
'-Infinity'
>>> json.dumps(float('nan'))
'NaN'
```

## Not covered on this page

- **Float repr:** The page shows floats like `1.0` and `2.0` in output but does not document the formatting rule. In CPython, floats are generally written using `float.__repr__`, which gives the shortest string that round-trips. Check the CPython source or `float.__repr__` documentation to confirm.

- **Empty list and dict with `indent`:** The page does not cover this. In CPython, `json.dumps([], indent=4)` returns `'[]'` and `json.dumps({}, indent=4)` returns `'{}'`, with no inner newlines. This is based on known behavior, not on this page.

>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='PROG')
>>> parser.add_argument('--foo', type=int)
>>> parser.parse_args(['--foo', 'spam'])

### `prog`
- Default: derived from how `__main__` was run. It is the base name of `sys.argv[0]` for a file, the interpreter name plus `sys.argv[0]` for a directory or zipfile, or the interpreter name plus `-m` plus the module name for `-m`.
- Override with `prog=`. Use `%(prog)s` in help text to reference it.
- Changed in 3.14: the default now reflects how `__main__` was actually executed.

```
>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='myprogram')
>>> parser.add_argument('--foo', help='foo of the %(prog)s program')
```

### `exit_on_error`
- Default `True`. Setting it to `False` lets you catch errors yourself:

```
>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(exit_on_error=False)
>>> parser.add_argument('--integers', type=int)
>>> try:
...     parser.parse_args('--integers a'.split())
... except argparse.ArgumentError:
...     print('Catching an argumentError')

- The visible text does not describe `-` as a plain positional argument. Its documented behavior is with `FileType`: `'-'` maps to `sys.stdin` for readable files and `sys.stdout` for writable ones.

>>> parser.add_argument('infile', type=argparse.FileType('r'))

- The callable takes a single string. If it raises `ArgumentTypeError`, `TypeError`, or `ValueError`, argparse catches it and shows a formatted error. Other exception types are not handled.

```
>>> def hyphenated(string):
...     return '-'.join([word[:4] for word in string.casefold().split()])
...

## `subprocess.run()` Key Arguments

```python
subprocess.run(args, *, stdin=None, input=None, stdout=None, stderr=None,
               capture_output=False, shell=False, cwd=None, timeout=None,
               check=False, encoding=None, errors=None, text=None,
               env=None, universal_newlines=None, **other_popen_kwargs)
```

Per the docs, `run()` waits for the command to finish and returns a `CompletedProcess` instance. `timeout`, `input`, `check`, and `capture_output` are handled by `run()` itself and are not passed to `Popen`.

### `args`
- Required. Should be a sequence of program arguments, which is generally preferred because the module handles quoting and escaping.
- A string is allowed only with `shell=True`, or when it names a program with no arguments.

### `capture_output`
- If true, stdout and stderr are captured, with both set to `PIPE` internally.
- Cannot be combined with `stdout` or `stderr`.
- To merge both streams, use `stdout=PIPE, stderr=STDOUT` instead.

```python
r = subprocess.run(["ls", "-l", "/dev/null"], capture_output=True)
print(r.stdout)  # b'crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 1, 3 ... /dev/null\n'
print(r.stderr)  # b''
```

### `text` / `encoding` / `errors` (and `universal_newlines`)
- Setting `encoding`, `errors`, or `text=True` opens stdin, stdout, and stderr in text mode. Without these, streams are binary.
- `text` was added in 3.7 as a clearer alias for `universal_newlines`, which is kept for backward compatibility.
- If `encoding` or `errors` is not given, the `io.TextIOWrapper` defaults apply.
- Line endings:
  - **stdout/stderr:** all line endings in the output are converted to `'\n'`. This is the universal-newlines behavior that normalizes `\r\n` (and `\r`) to `\n`.
  - **stdin:** `'\n'` in `input` is converted to `os.linesep`.
- In text mode, `input` must be `str`, and `stdout`/`stderr` in `CompletedProcess` are `str`.

```python
r = subprocess.run(["printf", "a\\r\\nb\\r\\n"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(repr(r.stdout))  # 'a\nb\n'
```

### Bytes mode (default)
- With none of `text`, `encoding`, `errors`, or `universal_newlines` set, `stdout`/`stderr` are `bytes`.
- No encoding or line-ending conversion is performed, so `\r\n` stays as-is.
- `input` must be a bytes sequence.
- Decoding is left to the application, since the encoding depends on the command.

```python
r = subprocess.run(["ls", "-l", "/dev/null"], capture_output=True)
data = r.stdout.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
```

### `cwd`
- Changes the child's working directory before execution. Accepts a string, bytes, or path-like object (bytes on Windows since 3.8).
- On POSIX, a relative executable path is resolved relative to `cwd`.

### `env`
- If not `None`, this mapping replaces the inherited environment entirely.
- Use `str` to `str` on any platform, or `bytes` to `bytes` on POSIX.
- It must include every variable the program needs.
- On Windows, side-by-side assemblies require a valid `%SystemRoot%` in `env`.

```python
import os
env = {**os.environ, "MY_VAR": "1"}  # copy, then add a variable
subprocess.run(["env"], env=env, text=True)
```

### `check`
- If true and the exit code is non-zero, raises `CalledProcessError`, which has `returncode`, `cmd`, `output`/`stdout`, and `stderr`.

```python
try:
    subprocess.run(["false"], check=True)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print(e.returncode)
```

### `timeout`
- Seconds, passed to `Popen.communicate()`.
- On expiry, the child is killed and waited for, then `TimeoutExpired` is raised. Its `output`/`stdout` and `stderr` attributes hold any captured output, as bytes regardless of `text`, or `None` if nothing was observed.
- Process creation itself may not be interruptible, so a timeout exception may come later than expected.

```python
try:
    subprocess.run(["sleep", "10"], timeout=2)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as e:
    print("timed out after", e.timeout, "s")
```

# Research report: csvledger (`python -m csvledger`)

The repo contains only `brief.md` and `contract.md` (git status was clean). I read both and the Python 3 docs pages listed under Sources. Items marked **[unverified]** were not stated on the docs pages I fetched. They come from known CPython behavior and should be confirmed with a quick local test. I did not create or modify any files.

## Key findings

1. **argparse errors.** `parser.error()` prints the usage text and then `PROG: error: <msg>` to stderr, and exits 2. The usage text comes first, so the contract's "last stderr line" regex `^csvledger( report| categorize)?: error: ` holds. With `prog='csvledger'`, a subparser's prog becomes `csvledger report`, which the contract allows.
2. **`--help` exit code.** The fetched page did not state the exit code. Argparse's help action exits 0 **[unverified]**, which matches AC1. Help goes to stdout.
3. **Subparser dispatch.** `add_subparsers(dest='command', required=True)` makes a missing subcommand a usage error with exit 2. `required` is keyword-only and has existed since 3.7. Without `required=True`, a bare `python -m csvledger` would fall through with `command=None`.
4. **`-` as a filename.** argparse treats a lone `-` as a positional argument. The docs only show it mapped to stdin/stdout when `type=argparse.FileType`.
   - Declare FILE as `nargs='+'` with no `type`, and never use `FileType`.
   - The spec should then open it with `open('-')` like any other path.
   - `--` ends option parsing, so a file named like a flag works as `-- -x.csv`.
5. **`type=` validation.** The callable receives one string. `ArgumentTypeError`, `TypeError` and `ValueError` become a normal exit-2 usage error. Other exceptions escape as a traceback.
   - For `--month`, write a validator that applies `re.fullmatch(r'\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])', s)`. It should raise `ArgumentTypeError` on failure.
   - Use `fullmatch` or `\Z` rather than `$`, because `$` also matches before a trailing `\n`. For example, `"2026-01\n"` passes `^...$` **[unverified]**. Likewise `\d` matches non-ASCII digits unless `re.ASCII` is set **[unverified]**.
   - `choices=['table','json']` is checked after type conversion, so `--format` gets exit 2 for free.
6. **Argparse's own output encoding.** Usage and error text goes through `sys.stderr`. Reconfiguring stdout does not change that, so the stderr handling in finding 9 matters for argparse messages too.
7. **`TextIOWrapper.reconfigure`.** Its signature is `reconfigure(*, encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None, line_buffering=None, write_through=None)`.
   - `encoding` and `newline` can't be changed after data has been read from the stream. Changing `encoding` after a write is allowed.
   - With `newline=None`, writing `\n` becomes `os.linesep` (`\r\n` on Windows). With `''` or `'\n'` there is no translation.
   - So `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding='utf-8', newline='\n')` is required for byte-exact output on Windows.
   - If `encoding` is given without `errors`, errors resets to `'strict'`.
   - Reconfigure before any output, and do it unconditionally (it is harmless on POSIX).
   - `sys.stdout` can be `None` under `pythonw`, or lack `reconfigure` if replaced by a `StringIO`. Guard with `hasattr` if the code is called from tests in-process.
8. **Windows stdout encoding.** For a console, Python uses UTF-8. For pipes and files it uses the ANSI codepage, for example cp1252. A non-ASCII description in table output would raise `UnicodeEncodeError` (a traceback) when piped, or be written in the wrong encoding, if stdout is not reconfigured. `PYTHONIOENCODING` is not a reliable fix because the caller controls the environment.
9. **stderr.** stderr's error handler is always `backslashreplace`, so it never raises `UnicodeEncodeError`.
   - On a Windows pipe, though, stderr uses the locale codepage. A path or message with characters outside that codepage is written as `\uXXXX` escapes, not as UTF-8.
   - Contract R11 only says stdout is UTF-8. To make stderr UTF-8 too, the spec can reconfigure it as `sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding='utf-8', errors='backslashreplace')` (or `'replace'`).
   - Tests must decode stderr with the same assumption, and should assert on ASCII-only paths and messages, or on bytes.
10. **Avoiding tracebacks.** Wrap the whole `main()` in these handlers:
    - `OSError`, which covers `FileNotFoundError`, `PermissionError`, `IsADirectoryError` and similar, gives "cannot read file".
    - `UnicodeDecodeError` gives "not valid UTF-8". It can surface during iteration, not only at `open`, so the whole read loop must be inside the `try`.
    - `csv.Error` should be handled too; the contract is silent on it. Examples are a field larger than the field-size limit, or a NUL byte **[unverified]**. Map these to a clean exit 3/4 with a row-level message.
    - `ValueError` also needs care. `datetime.date(...)` raises it for a day like 02-30, and Decimal conversion can too.
    - A catch-all `Exception` returning exit 1 matches the "reserved for unexpected internal error" row, but it should still print only a one-line `csvledger: error:` message.
    - `sys.exit(2)` from argparse is a `SystemExit`, not an `Exception`, so it passes through a broad `except Exception`.
    - `BrokenPipeError` on stdout is an edge case to consider.
11. **BOM and CSV reading.** `encoding='utf-8-sig'` strips an optional BOM.
    - Open with `newline=''`, because the csv docs say embedded newlines in quoted fields are mishandled otherwise.
    - `reader.line_num` counts lines read from the source, not records. A quoted multi-line field therefore makes `line_num` larger than the record count. The contract says to use `line_num` after reading the record, which is consistent.
    - Blank lines come back as `[]` **[unverified]**, which matches the "zero fields are skipped" rule.
    - A 0-byte file yields no header row, which is the "missing header" case.
    - A file containing only a BOM, or only blank lines, also yields no non-empty header. The contract is ambiguous about whether a blank line 1 is the header or is skipped, so the spec should state which.
    - The csv module's default `strict=False` is lenient with stray quotes. The contract says to use defaults, so don't set `strict`.
12. **JSON output.** `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` has these properties:
    - With `indent` set, the separators default to `(',', ': ')`, so there is no trailing whitespace. This has held since 3.4.
    - Key order follows insertion order, and no `sort_keys` is needed since the contract fixes the key order.
    - The result has no trailing newline, so append `\n`.
    - Empty containers print as `[]` and `{}` **[unverified]**. `{"months": []}` therefore prints as `{` `"months": []` `}` across three lines, not on one line. The contract's "Empty: `{"months": []}`" is a logical description, so the spec should show the exact bytes.
    - With `ensure_ascii=False`, only `"`, `\` and control characters U+0000 to U+001F are escaped. A description containing a lone surrogate can't occur here after strict UTF-8 decoding.
    - Money values are strings, so no float or `Decimal` serialization issue arises. A `Decimal` passed directly would raise `TypeError`.
13. **Table alignment.** `len()` counts code points, so wide CJK characters and combining marks misalign visually. The contract explicitly accepts this. Use `str.ljust` and `str.rjust`, which also count code points. Right-strip each line after joining with two spaces, as the contract says.
14. **Oracle check.** Hand-checking O1 and O5 against the contract shows the intended arithmetic.
    - In O1, `-45.10 + -12.005 = -57.105`, which rounds half up (away from zero for negatives) to `-57.11`.
    - `ROUND_HALF_UP` in `decimal` rounds ties away from zero, so `-57.105` becomes `-57.11`, as the oracle shows.
    - In O5, Tiny has income `0.005 + 0.005 = 0.010`, displayed `0.01`.
    - Tiny expenses are `-0.004`, which rounds to `-0.00` and must print `0.00`.
    - Tiny net is `0.006`, displayed `0.01`.
    - Misc has income `0.125`, displayed `0.13`, and expenses `-0.125`, displayed `-0.13`. Its net is `0.00`.
    - Sums must stay unrounded and be formatted once.
15. **Amount edge cases.** Amounts like `-12.005` and `0.125` have more than 2 decimals, and the regex allows arbitrarily many.
    - `Decimal("-0")`, `0.00` and `-0.000` are all zero, and `-0` compares equal to 0.
    - The dedup key uses the "numeric amount value" (R5), so `-4.5` equals `-4.50`. `Decimal("-4.5") == Decimal("-4.50")` is True, and their hashes are equal too. A tuple key `(date, desc.strip(), amount)` therefore works. Don't key on the string form.
    - Zero-valued `Decimal("0")` and `Decimal("-0")` also hash equal.
    - Very long digit strings are fine in `Decimal`, but the default context precision of 28 digits applies to arithmetic. A value with more than 28 significant digits would be rounded during summation, which breaks "exact". The spec should either set a large precision with `localcontext` or `getcontext().prec`, or state that amounts are limited.
    - `quantize` can raise `InvalidOperation` if the result has more digits than the precision, for the same reason.
16. **Date validation.** The regex `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` comes first, then calendar validity. `\d` matches Unicode digits, and `date.fromisoformat` is stricter than that in some cases, so use `re.ASCII` or `[0-9]`. `$` also matches before a trailing newline, which the stripped value won't have. Year `0000` matches the regex but is invalid for `datetime.date` (minimum year 1), so it should give "invalid date".
17. **Regex rules.** `re.search(pattern, description, re.IGNORECASE)` is applied to the description. `contains` uses `casefold()` on both sides. Compile at load time and catch `re.error` for "invalid regex". Compiling very pathological patterns may raise `RecursionError` or `OverflowError` **[unverified]**, so the catch could be broader than `re.error`.
18. **Priority parsing.** `^-?\d+$` allows huge integers, and `int()` handles them, but Python 3.11+ limits int string conversion to 4300 digits by default, raising `ValueError`. This is an edge case the spec could mention and treat as "invalid priority".
19. **Subprocess testing.**
    - `subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, cwd=..., env=..., timeout=...)` defaults to bytes mode. Bytes mode does no newline translation, which gives the byte-exact comparison the contract needs.
    - With `text=True`, `\r\n` and `\r` in output become `\n`, which would mask a stray `\r` bug. AC10 ("contains no `\r`") can't be tested in text mode.
    - `stdin` input is irrelevant because stdin is never read. Passing `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL` makes sure a test would fail or hang loudly if the tool tried to read it.
    - `env`, when given, replaces the whole environment. On Windows it must keep `SystemRoot`, so use `{**os.environ, ...}`.
    - Use `[sys.executable, "-m", "csvledger", ...]` with `cwd` set to the repo root. `-m` puts the current directory on `sys.path[0]`, which is how the package is found.
    - `-I` or `-P` would remove the cwd from `sys.path` and break `-m csvledger`, so don't use them for the tool itself. They are only for running untrusted downloaded scripts.
    - To exercise the "paths are the argv string" rule, tests should run with `cwd=tmp_path` and relative file names. In that case the repo root has to be on `PYTHONPATH` through `env`. The contract says run from the repo root, so decide which approach the tests take, and note the trade-off.
20. **Writing test fixtures.**
    - Fixtures should be written with `Path.write_bytes(b"...")` to control exact bytes, including `\r\n`, BOM and invalid UTF-8. `write_text` on Windows translates `\n` to `\r\n` unless `newline=` is passed. The docs page I fetched said nothing about this, so it's from Python's `Path.write_text` behavior **[unverified]** (the `newline` parameter was added in 3.10).
    - Oracle expected output should be stored as bytes or as a string compared with `.encode("utf-8")`, never read from a text-mode file that may be translated. Also check `.gitattributes`/autocrlf: a Windows checkout of fixture files with autocrlf would corrupt expected bytes. The repo has a `.gitignore` but I did not find `.gitattributes`.
    - `tmp_path` gives each test its own `pathlib.Path` temp directory, and its basename can contain non-ASCII characters only if the user's temp path does. For non-ASCII path tests, create a subdirectory or file with an explicit non-ASCII name inside `tmp_path`.
21. **`__main__.py` layout.** `python -m csvledger` runs `csvledger/__main__.py` as `__main__` after importing the package. A flat layout means:
    - `csvledger/__init__.py` (can be near-empty)
    - `csvledger/__main__.py` (thin: `from .cli import main`, then `sys.exit(main())`, guarded by `if __name__ == "__main__":`)
    - `csvledger/cli.py` (argparse, `main(argv=None) -> int`)
    - Separate modules for CSV loading, rules, aggregation and formatting.
    - `main()` should return an int, so tests can call it in-process.
    - Relative imports work under `-m` because the package is imported first.
    - `prog` must be set explicitly to `'csvledger'`, because without it argparse would derive `__main__.py` or similar from `sys.argv[0]`. The docs say the default depends on how `__main__` was run, and it changed in 3.14 to reflect how it was actually run.
    - Tests live in `tests/` at the repo root, with a `conftest.py` that locates the repo root.
22. **No locale use.** R11 forbids the locale. Avoid `locale` and `str.format` with `n`, use `format(q, "f")` for money, and use plain `sorted()` on code points for categories. Don't use `str.lower()` for sorting. `casefold` is only for `contains` matching.

## Constraints the spec MUST respect

- Python 3.11+, stdlib only, with pytest for tests only. `csvledger/` is at the repo root with no `src/`, and the entry point is `python -m csvledger` from the repo root.
- argparse `prog='csvledger'`, subcommands `report` and `categorize`, and `--help` exits 0. Usage errors exit 2: unknown flag, missing FILE, bad `--format` or `--month`.
- `--month` must match `^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$`, otherwise exit 2.
- The last stderr line of a usage error must match `^csvledger( report| categorize)?: error: `.
- `-` is an ordinary filename and stdin is never read.
- stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
- stdout is empty on any exit 3 or 4. This means buffering all output until all inputs are parsed and validated.
- Load order is rules first, then files in argument order, and the first error wins.
- The error line format is `csvledger: error: <path>[:<line>]: <msg>` on a single line, with `<path>` exactly as given in argv.
- The row-check and header-check orders in the contract are fixed.
- Exit codes are 0, 1 (never intentional), 2, 3 and 4 as in the contract's table.
- The duplicate warning goes to stderr after stdout output. Dedup runs over all rows of all files before the `--month` filter, and N counts all duplicates regardless of `--month`.
- Money is `decimal.Decimal`, and sums are unrounded. Display is quantized once with `ROUND_HALF_UP`, and `0.00` is never shown as `-0.00`.
- JSON uses `indent=2, ensure_ascii=False` plus a trailing `\n`, with the key order specified.
- Table widths use `len()` on code points, separators are two spaces, lines are right-stripped, and the dash line is included.
- Output is byte-identical across runs and platforms, with no `\r`.
